title: Micro-Method Proliferation (Classitis / Fragmented Logic)
pattern: Splitting a highly cohesive, simple mathematical or logical expression into an excessive number of microscopic, parameterless, or thin helper functions.
why_bad: Fragmenting logic across too many tiny functions increases semantic distance and forces the reader to constantly hop between declarations. The overhead of context switching hurts readability, while providing zero potential for code reuse or alternative polymorphism.
detection: Identify functions containing only 1-2 lines of trivial operations (e.g., a single addition or comparison) that are only invoked by a single caller within the same scope.
counterexample: Functions implementing standard library traits (like `PartialEq` or `Default`) where 1-line bodies are required by the contract.
source: *John K. Ousterhout - A Philosophy of Software Design (2018)*, Chapter 4, "Modules Should Be Deep" (Classitis, p. 25); *Martin Fowler - Refactoring (1999)*, Chapter 3, "Lazy Class" and Chapter 6, "Inline Method".
